Issued at 515 AM CDT Tue Jul 28 2026

Upper level ridge axis lies across eastern Montana/Wyoming 
early this morning. A benign surface pattern is analyzed over 
the Northern Plains, with mesoscale high pressure from southern 
Manitoba into northeast North Dakota. Dense fog has developed 
along and northeast of Highway 52, as far south as the Highway 
200 corridor. A Dense Fog Advisory remains in effect for these 
areas until 10 AM CDT. Meanwhile, weak warm air/moisture 
advection underneath the right entrance region of an upper level
jet has initiated isolated showers with an occasional 
thunderstorm from the northern James River Valley to between 
Lake Oahe and the southern James River Valley. This convection 
may continue meandering through this part of the state into the 
mid/late morning hours before dissipating, but forecast 
confidence is low as this convection was not modeled very well. 

The upper level ridge will remain in place today. High 
temperatures should return to the 90s to near 100 with lesser 
cloud cover than yesterday. Smoke aloft remains a wild card 
though, and could keep temperatures a few degrees cooler. A 
mention of patchy smoke was maintained in the forecast through 
tonight in continuity with HRRR/RAP near-surface smoke guidance,
although the correlation between modeled smoke concentrations 
and observed visibility is subjectively verifying with mixed 
results at best. Nevertheless, confidence remains high in at 
least some amount of smoke in the air through the middle of the 
week, whether it be aloft or at the surface. The upper ridge 
continues to build and pivots eastward on Wednesday ahead of 
shortwave energy ejecting off the Northern Rockies, bringing the
thermal ridge back into the western Dakotas. The NBM shows high
confidence in high temperatures around 100 across much of 
western and central North Dakota, with maximum heat indices also
around 100 along and to the west and south of the Missouri 
River Valley.

With weak disturbances continuing to round the top of the ridge
and forecast highs near convective temperatures, occasional 
isolated showers and thunderstorms cannot be ruled out this 
afternoon and evening. We are broadly not carrying mentionable 
PoPs, as the point-specific probability for a shower or storm 
at any given location is less than 15 percent. But in general, 
CAMs would indicate relatively higher odds of convection 
initiating across southern and eastern North Dakota than to the 
north and west. CAPE is forecast to decrease across western 
North Dakota this afternoon, but the eastern half of the state 
could see 1000-2000 J/kg CAPE with around 25-30 kts of deep 
layer shear during the late afternoon and early evening. 
Therefore, a stronger storm cannot be ruled out in the James 
River Valley over the aforementioned timeframe, which a couple 
CAMs have been consistently simulating. 

Through Wednesday morning, a turning of the low level wind 
field to southwesterly will bring warm air/moisture advection 
into western and central North Dakota. CAMs indicate a low 
probability of shower and thunderstorm development in response 
to this forcing, with any storms likely remaining elevated and 
sub-severe. There is a very low probability scenario though 
where this activity becomes rooted in the boundary layer before 
departing into eastern North Dakota early Wednesday afternoon. 
The greater focus for strong to severe convection will be along 
a lee trough near the MT/ND border mid Wednesday afternoon. 
Model guidance is consistent in initiating deep moist convection
by late afternoon, albeit with timing and coverage discrepancies.
Storm mode could be mixed initially, with shear vectors more 
perpendicular to the lee trough in southern North Dakota, but 
more parallel to it farther north. Upscale growth into clusters 
is favored as storms propagate eastward into central North 
Dakota late Wednesday evening into the overnight hours, with 
more favorable maintenance of convection across the north where 
buoyancy, shear, and forcing could all be stronger. The tornado 
risk appears very low, but a favorable setup could briefly 
emerge in far northwest North Dakota early Wednesday evening. 
However, current HRRR/RAP hodographs at Crosby show crosswise 
vorticity in the 0-1 km layer, rendering tornadogenesis less 
favorable. 

Medium chances for showers and thunderstorms continue on 
Thursday as broad mid level shortwave troughing in the middle 
of the longwave ridge stalls over the Northern Plains. A medium 
to high CAPE and low to moderate shear environment could support
a few severe storms Thursday afternoon and evening, but details
remain uncertain. A slight cool down is expected on Thursday, 
but with highs remaining in the mid 80s to mid 90s. Similar high
temperatures carry into Friday as the shortwave dives southeast
into the Upper Mississippi and Lower Missouri River Valleys.
